title: FaultDesk: AI fault-report desk for facility-service firms that look after housing co-ops (Sweden first)
source: Top 50 research (Nov 2026): reframed from ideas dropped from the Top 25 report, plus new web research
summary: Facility-service firms that maintain Swedish housing co-ops (BRF) get fault reports from residents by phone, email and apps. FaultDesk sorts each report by urgency, asks for photos, checks if the repair is the resident's or the co-op's responsibility, and creates the work order.
hook: "Half the calls are about things the resident must fix themselves. But we only find out after we have sent a technician."
story:
**Johan owns a 25-person property-care firm (fastighetsskötsel) in Stockholm** that looks after **80 housing co-ops with about 3,500 flats**. Fault reports arrive everywhere: phone calls, emails, the co-op board's app, notes in the stairwell. Two office staff type them into the work-order system.

Many reports are about things the **resident must pay for under the co-op's responsibility list** (a dripping tap inside the flat, a broken dishwasher). Technicians drive out, then the co-op refuses to pay. Real emergencies, like a water leak at night, get mixed with "the light in the laundry room is broken". Johan wants every report sorted, completed with a photo and checked against the co-op's rules **before** a technician is sent.
whyNow: About one in five Swedish households lives in a co-op flat, and co-op boards push their facility firms for faster answers and monthly reporting. AI can now read a resident's message and the co-op's own responsibility list in Swedish, which was not practical two years ago.
evidence: 21% of Swedish households live in co-op (bostadsrätt) flats, about 1 million households, at the end of 2025 [SCB, Hushållens boende 2025]
German startup Lette claims more than 60% of service and maintenance requests can be handled automatically (vendor claim) [Startbase]
Capital in property-maintenance AI is concentrated in big US players such as EliseAI (reported $4B valuation), which do not serve small Nordic facility firms [CRE Daily via Top 25 report]
Swedish co-op apps such as Boappa and Ourliving let residents send fault reports to the board, but do not triage them or check responsibility [Boappa guide / App Store]

whyReal.title: Wasted technician trips cost money
whyReal.text: Every trip to fix something the resident must pay for, or that needed a different trade, costs the firm time and creates billing fights with the co-op.

whyReal.title: Jonatan knows this buyer
whyReal.text: Facility and property-care firms are his industry. He can reach owners by phone in Swedish and English.

whyReal.title: Narrower and safer than general maintenance AI
whyReal.text: General property-maintenance triage was dropped from the Top 25 because funded US startups compete. Swedish co-ops, their responsibility lists and small facility firms are a niche they ignore.

whyReal.title: Same buyer as SubDocs and CleanProof
whyReal.text: A facility firm using FaultDesk is a natural customer for the top-ranked document and inspection ideas.

whoPays.label: Customer
whoPays.text: Facility-service and property-care firms with 5–100 staff that maintain housing co-ops and small rental buildings.

whoPays.label: Buyer
whoPays.text: The owner or operations manager of the facility firm.

whoPays.label: Start market
whoPays.text: Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö, then Norway and Finland (similar co-op models).

solution.title: One inbox for all reports
solution.text: a web form and QR code for each building, an email address and an SMS number feed one queue.

solution.title: AI triage
solution.text: each report is sorted into trade (plumbing, electrical, locks, laundry), urgency (emergency, this week, planned) and building.

solution.title: Asks for what is missing
solution.text: the resident gets an automatic reply asking for a photo, flat number or access time.

solution.title: Responsibility check
solution.text: FaultDesk compares the fault with the co-op's own responsibility list (ansvarsfördelning) and marks it "co-op pays", "resident pays" or "check".

solution.title: Work order and updates
solution.text: a ready work order goes to the firm's system or technician app; residents get status messages.

solution.title: Monthly board report
solution.text: each co-op board gets a short report: faults, response times, costs, recurring problems.

must: Building QR codes and web fault form
AI triage by trade, urgency and building
Upload of each co-op's responsibility list and automatic check
Work-order board with status updates to residents
later: Integration with work-order systems used by Swedish facility firms

techStack: LLM for Swedish text triage and rule checking
Simple mobile web app for technicians

Intake form, email/SMS, AI triage, responsibility check.
Work-order board, resident updates, board report, payments.
First 3 paying firms; measure wasted trips saved.

risks.answer: Anything that might be urgent (water, gas, smoke, locked out) always goes to a human phone number at once; AI never closes emergencies.
Accept a Nordic-first market, then expand with the same engine to cleaning and facility firms elsewhere.

risks.risk: Firms already use a work-order system
risks.answer: Act as the intake layer and push orders into their system instead of replacing it.
FaultDesk handles written reports and rules; phone answering can be a later add-on, not the core.

questions: How many fault reports do you get per week, and through which channels?
How often does a technician go out for something the resident should pay for?
How do you know each co-op's responsibility rules today?
What system do you use for work orders, and who types reports into it?
Would €99–199 a month be worth it if it cut wasted trips and typing? Who decides?

numbers.competition: Co-op apps and big systems, no triage for facility firms
